newsitem.title: GERMANY: German position as financial centre secure-Gaddum.
newsitem.headline: German position as financial centre secure-Gaddum.

text.p: Germany's position as a global financial centre is assured even after the start of Europe's currency union, a senior Bundesbank official said on Monday, shrugging off criticisms the German market is too provincial.

Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum told the German daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung that when compared with its European rivals before the start of EMU, Germany occupied a competitive position.
While Gaddum acknowledged that it is impossible to unseat London as Europe's largest financial centre overnight, he stressed that Germany was on level ground with Paris.

"We offer benchmark paper and are therefore well placed," Gaddum told the newspaper, adding that the German government's pledge to consider offering 30-year dated paper helped complete the yield curve structure.
Germany introduced short-term debt only last summer, agreeing at that time to venture both into longer and shorter-dated maturities, away from the nation's preferred five and 10-year paper.

Gaddum also highlighted state-of-the-art technology employed in German markets. "In terms on technology, Frankfurt can compete with the best financial centres," Gaddum said, adding however more improvements needed to be made in the share market.
Gaddum shrugged off banks' demands that Germany change its system of issuing paper from the current two-pronged banking consortium and the public auction, following one day later.
Some banks have complained that the current system discriminates against some banks but Gaddum said the consortium received only 6.5 percent of all paper issued last year.
"Considering this fact, it is curious that this practice is being portrayed as a hindrance," Gaddum said.

He noted that other nations who use a primary dealership system, where only a few banks buy the paper and then act like a wholesaler distributing it on, have a much smaller number participating in the refunding auctions.
Addressing banks' criticism of the current system, Gaddum said, "not everything that is considered to be un-modern can be seen to affect the German market negatively."
Gaddum also said the Bundesbank might play a different role after the the European central bank, to be located in Frankfurt, will take over handling monetary policy for Europe.
